Why I Build Software

The deepest satisfaction I find in programming is not that a program runs, or that a difficult implementation is complete. It is the moment when work made with thought and care becomes useful in another person's day: a search becomes possible, a repeated task becomes lighter, an answer becomes more reliable, or someone reaches what they needed with less difficulty.

An employer or a client makes a project possible and deserves honest, competent work. But a system ultimately meets human lives through the people who use it, depend on it or use it to help someone else. Their time, attention, confidence and access to information give software its practical meaning.

I write software to shorten paths between people and worthwhile outcomes. The gratification is quiet but lasting: knowing that something I built performed a small, real service in the world.

Software As A Bridge

Software can also be a bridge.

A small automation can return hours of life.
A well-conceived system can reduce daily friction.
A clear interface can lessen operational anxiety.
An integration can bring people and processes closer together.

In the end, software engineering is also about shortening paths.

A Small Library System

In 2002, soon after graduating, I built one of my first programs for the library of an educational institution. The library already had a legacy system: it issued an auto-incremented number that was printed, attached to each book and used as the prevailing order on the shelves. That identified items, but did little to place related works together.

I introduced a three-part numeric classification: category, work and copy. A book could be positioned near others on the same subject, and a new edition or additional copy of a work could be placed immediately after its peers. The change was simple to state, but tangible in use: the physical collection began to express affinity rather than only order of arrival.

The system provided screens for recording books and their indexes, and allowed keyword searches through that indexed content. It also supported loans and returns, reported overdue items and indicated expected return dates. The librarian used this information to locate relevant material and inform people interested in a borrowed work when it might become available.

I also built an ASP 3 page with the idea of making consultation available from the laboratories. It was not put into service there. The actual result was more modest and more honest: access still passed through the librarian. Yet the benefit of the delivered system was real. It strengthened her ability to guide students through the collection, answer questions and connect a person with a book that could help them learn.

That experience remains important to me because it gives a human scale to the profession. A system does not need a vast audience or fashionable technology to justify pride in the work. Sometimes satisfaction comes from improving one person's work so that she can better serve many others, and from knowing that the care placed in structure, search and information reached people in a practical way.

Consequences For Engineering

This understanding of satisfaction has practical consequences:

  • A feature is incomplete if it exists technically but is difficult for its intended user to find, understand or trust.
  • A user may be the professional who mediates a service for others; improving that person's work can improve many people's access and experience.
  • A small application deserves clear data handling, dependable behavior and usable documentation when people rely on it.
  • Performance, availability and accessible interaction matter because delay, outage and exclusion are experienced by people, not by architecture diagrams.
  • A technical shortcut is not harmless when it transfers recurring work, confusion or risk to users or maintainers.
  • Success is not measured only by delivery; it includes whether the software continues to serve its purpose responsibly.

Professional Boundary

Being oriented toward users does not mean ignoring legitimate business needs, budgets, deadlines or the judgment of colleagues. Software is produced inside real organizations with competing constraints. It means that, when discussing tradeoffs, the effect on the person who uses or depends on the system remains visible and is not treated as an afterthought. It also means describing our own work honestly: an unrealized interface is not a delivered benefit, while a less visible improvement in someone's daily service is still worth recognizing.

The rest of this book translates that position into daily engineering practice.
